meta.source: Luminari WA Master Template v1.0 — Northwest Hope Foundation

steps.action: Document the violation with timestamp. Photograph the issue. Keep all correspondence with landlord in writing (text or email). Note dates, times, temperatures if applicable.
steps.notes: Creates paper trail for all subsequent steps

steps.action: Send written notice (text or email) to landlord stating the violation, citing RCW 59.18. Give landlord reasonable time to remedy.
File complaint with Seattle Office of Housing (city), or King County Code Enforcement, or WA Attorney General Renters' Rights Hotline.
steps.state_agency: Seattle Office of Housing / King County Code Enforcement / WA AG Renters' Rights
steps.notes: City, county, or state depending on jurisdiction

steps.action: Request city or county housing inspection. Inspection report becomes official documentation.
steps.state_agency: Seattle Office of Housing / King County Code Enforcement
steps.notes: Inspection report is critical evidence for legal proceedings

steps.action: Contact Housing Justice Project (free eviction defense) or Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline. Consider rent withholding remedy under RCW 59.18.115.
steps.deadline: If landlord does not remedy within reasonable time
steps.notes: Free legal help at courthouse for eviction defense

steps.action: File complaint with WA Attorney General Consumer Protection Division. If health/safety threat, contact Seattle-King County Public Health.
steps.state_agency: WA Attorney General Consumer Protection / Seattle-King County Public Health
steps.deadline: If agency does not respond within 30 days
steps.notes: Escalation step — for systemic or unresolved violations

steps.action: Collect denial letter, Explanation of Benefits (EOB), original claim, and all correspondence. Note exact denial language and reason code.
steps.notes: Denial letter contains appeal deadline — do not miss it

steps.action: File internal appeal with insurer within the deadline stated in denial letter (typically 180 days for ACA plans). Request full claims file.
steps.documents_needed: Written appeal letter, supporting medical records
steps.deadline: Before deadline in denial letter (typically 180 days for ACA plans)
steps.notes: Internal appeal is required before external review in most cases

steps.action: Get treating physician to write letter of medical necessity. Get clinical notes and peer-reviewed evidence supporting the treatment.
steps.documents_needed: Physician letter, clinical notes, peer-reviewed evidence
steps.notes: Physician support letter is the strongest evidence for medical necessity appeals

steps.action: If internal appeal denied, request Independent Review Organization (IRO) external review through WA Office of Insurance Commissioner.
steps.documents_needed: Internal appeal denial, all medical documentation
steps.deadline: Within 4 months of internal appeal denial (WA law)
steps.notes: IRO decision is binding on insurer. OIC administers the process.

steps.action: File formal complaint with WA OIC if insurer acted in bad faith, delayed processing, or violated WA insurance regulations.
steps.documents_needed: Full documentation package including all denials and appeals
steps.deadline: No strict deadline — but file promptly
steps.notes: OIC investigates and can fine insurers. Complaint creates regulatory record.

steps.action: Seek legal help. Contact NJP CLEAR hotline or private insurance bad faith attorney. Consider filing with CFPB for billing disputes on ERISA plans.
steps.deadline: If OIC complaint does not resolve within 60 days
steps.notes: Private attorneys often take insurance bad faith cases on contingency

steps.action: Calculate unpaid wages using pay stubs, time records, or personal records. Document specific dates, hours worked, amounts paid vs. owed.
steps.documents_needed: Pay stubs, time records, offer letter
steps.notes: WA statute of limitations: 3 years for wage claims

steps.action: Send written demand to employer for unpaid wages. Keep copy. Creates record and sometimes resolves without agency involvement.
steps.notes: Written demand creates paper trail and may resolve issue directly

steps.action: File wage complaint with WA Department of Labor & Industries, Labor Standards Program. Free. L&I investigates and can recover wages + penalties.
steps.state_agency: WA Department of Labor & Industries — Labor Standards
steps.notes: L&I can recover wages plus penalties. Free to file.

steps.action: File complaint with federal Wage and Hour Division (WHD) if federal law applies (FLSA — interstate commerce, federal contractors, etc.).
steps.state_agency: US DOL Wage and Hour Division
steps.notes: Can dual-file with L&I and DOL WHD

steps.action: Seek legal help. Contact NJP CLEAR hotline or Unemployment Law Project. Private attorney option: wage theft cases often taken on contingency.
steps.deadline: If L&I investigation stalls or employer retaliates
steps.notes: Private attorneys often take wage theft on contingency

steps.action: If employer retaliates for filing complaint, file retaliation complaint with L&I within 180 days. Retaliation is separately actionable.
steps.notes: Retaliation is separately unlawful — file even if original claim is pending

steps.action: If immediate danger, call 911. If not immediate, document observations: dates, injuries, statements, witness names.
steps.notes: Safety first — document only when safe to do so

steps.action: Call WA Adult Protective Services hotline. APS investigates abuse of vulnerable adults in any setting.
steps.deadline: Within 24 hours — APS has legal authority to investigate
steps.notes: APS hotline is 24/7. Mandatory reporters must report within 48 hours.

steps.action: Call WA Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Ombudsman advocates specifically for nursing home and assisted living residents. Free and confidential.
steps.notes: Free, confidential, resident-centered advocacy

steps.action: File complaint with WA DSHS Residential Care Services (RCS). RCS licenses and inspects care facilities.
steps.notes: RCS investigates licensing violations and care standards

steps.action: If Medicare/Medicaid facility, file complaint with CMS. Federal oversight.
steps.documents_needed: Facility name, Medicare/Medicaid certification number if known
steps.notes: Federal jurisdiction for Medicare/Medicaid certified facilities

steps.action: Seek legal help. Contact Elder Law Program at ELAP, NJP CLEAR hotline, or private elder law attorney. Consider guardianship review if financial exploitation.
steps.deadline: If pattern of abuse or financial exploitation suspected
steps.notes: Financial exploitation may require guardianship review

steps.action: Get the denial notice in writing. Note the reason code, date, and appeal deadline. WA requires written notice with appeal rights.
steps.notes: Denial notice contains the appeal deadline — do not miss it

steps.action: File request for Administrative Fair Hearing with DSHS Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH). Deadline: 90 days from denial date for most WA benefits.
steps.state_agency: WA DSHS Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH)
steps.deadline: Within 90 days — benefits may continue during appeal if requested
steps.notes: Fair hearing is a legal right — free process

steps.action: At same time as hearing request, request that benefits continue while appeal is pending. WA allows this if timely requested.
steps.deadline: Must request at time of appeal
steps.notes: Benefits continuation is critical — prevents gap in coverage during appeal

steps.action: Gather documents supporting eligibility: income records, medical records, housing records, anything contradicting denial reason.
steps.notes: Focus evidence on the specific reason for denial

steps.action: Contact NJP CLEAR hotline or Solid Ground Benefits Legal Help. Free representation at fair hearings available.
steps.deadline: As soon as possible after receiving denial
steps.notes: Free legal representation at fair hearings is available for qualifying individuals

steps.action: If hearing decision adverse, appeal to Superior Court. File complaint with DSHS constituent services and state legislators if systemic error.
steps.state_agency: WA Superior Court / DSHS Constituent Services / State Legislature
steps.notes: Escalation for systemic agency errors — legislative pressure can be effective

steps.action: Write down dates, incidents, witnesses, what was said or done. Keep all relevant emails, texts, performance reviews, HR correspondence.
steps.notes: Contemporaneous notes are strong evidence — write them the same day

steps.action: File complaint with HR or supervisor (if not the problem). Creates internal record. Note HR's response and timeline.
steps.deadline: Per company policy — before external filing in most cases
steps.notes: Internal complaint creates record but is not legally required before filing with WSHRC

steps.action: File complaint with WA State Human Rights Commission within 6 months of last discriminatory act. WSHRC investigates discrimination in employment.
steps.documents_needed: Written complaint with dates and incidents
steps.deadline: Within 6 months — this deadline is strict
steps.notes: WSHRC has broader protections than federal law in some areas

steps.action: File charge with federal EEOC within 300 days. Dual-file with WSHRC if possible. EEOC required before federal lawsuit.
steps.deadline: Within 300 days — can dual-file with WSHRC
steps.notes: EEOC charge is prerequisite for federal discrimination lawsuit

steps.action: Document any retaliation after filing complaint. File separate retaliation charge with WSHRC/EEOC. Retaliation is separately unlawful.
steps.notes: Retaliation is separately unlawful — file even if original claim is pending

steps.action: Seek legal help. Contact NJP CLEAR hotline or ACLU-WA. For unpaid wages component, contact L&I. Private employment attorneys often work on contingency.
steps.notes: Private employment attorneys often take discrimination cases on contingency
